title: The Economy of Christ and the Salvation of Women
english: And then, the hidden and economic [plan] which is for the sake of us all, delivered him. And where the economic [plan] preceded, it said: Jesus Christ the man. It approached the God-befitting [manner] and did not say 'the one delivered,' but 'the one who gave himself as a ransom for all.' And he says writing to the Galatians in this way: 'But now I live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God who loved me and gave himself for me' (Galatians 2:20). Why then are these things so skillfully crafted? And after running through all the harmony of the most God-befitting [words] spoken, having been added to the Jewish blindness and triviality, the children of Nestorius present the idea of the Christ being delivered or being raised by the Father, and they attempt through these, as it seems to them, not to show him to be a true God after he became truly man.

Regarding 1 Timothy 2:14-15: Because this woman has come into transgression, she will be saved through the children she will have and the descendants who will accomplish piety. What then, if she does not have children, or if she does have them but they are not males? But if indeed some are born, they are born of the common race; through which it is said universally that the transgression belongs to the female race. For if one is the cause for all of evil, how is it not fitting that the many should undo through the generation of the pious the evil that was brought upon them by one woman, since Christ has given the beginning of the undoing through himself? How then will the woman be saved? From the transgression and the disobedience; so that she must also have her own accomplishments, so that when the disobedience is forgiven, she is not condemned for other sins. It is not simply said to her: she will be saved through childbearing, but so that the mothers, having the children, may rear them in all piety and righteousness so as to be saved. To be saved through childbearing—not by means of which the woman transgressed, she is not judged, but she will be saved as a mother of those who obey, that is, according to the logic of obedience, since she has other own accomplishments through which she is saved. And this he says, as we have said, so that the mothers may rear the children in piety. From the reproach of the transgression she will be saved through childbearing. For this the apostle says, not to reproach, but to exhort toward piety and toward rearing the children in faith.

Regarding 1 Timothy 3:1: He did not say of honor, he did not say of wielding a spear, but of a good work, such as a good means, a good labor for the protection of the churches. If anyone aspires to the oversight, he desires a good work. He conceded not that of desire, but that of fitness, so that someone might equip himself for the fitness of oversight; rather, it is an exhortation to a good life, the entrance of desire, and just as a provision becomes for good works and the most beautiful life, so that glories have restrained the desire through...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Desire, Conduct, and the Manifestation of Christ
english: He is turned away from more things by being urged toward desire, rather than toward suitability, so that one might equip himself for the suitability of oversight through good works and faith. Rather, the entrance of desire is an exhortation to a good life. And desire is like an entrance into good works and the most beautiful life. So many things are enumerated as must belong to the bishop; it is enough to turn away [from bad things] so as to have surrendered desire to glories, by which he says what kind of man the bishop must be, and he turns away more.

Regarding 1 Tim 3:2, he most excellently exhorts, addressing in part the kinds of those living an ungraspable life. He does not accuse of striking, but the irrational one is moved; for a just charge rebukes, but an irrational accusation blames.

Regarding 1 Tim 3:16, instead of 'he was manifested in the flesh, but was justified in the spirit' [living] according to a certain conduct. For if indeed he was in the flesh, but was not conducting himself according to the flesh, but subjected the flesh to the spirit, opening for us the way of righteousness. Or this also he says, that while the Spirit was making signs, Christ was being justified according to our confession and faith. He was manifested to angels. Who? The crucified Christ. But he does not say this, that the angels do not see his divinity; for the Savior himself said that the angels see the face of my Father who is in the heavens. But when he says, 'No one has ever seen God,' it is evident that he has not seen [Him] as He is, but as far as it is possible to see, both for angel and man. Therefore God is invisible to both angels and men, but he was manifested through the economy. The church on earth was justified in the spirit through confession. This is similar to 'that you might be justified in your words and overcome when you are being judged'; for while the Spirit was making signs, he was being justified according to our confession and the faith of those believing. He who came for the salvation of men was manifested to angels; through this he showed that the divinity of the Only-Begotten is invisible to angels, but he was manifested to them through the flesh. He was taken up in glory; upon the clouds, he says.

Regarding 1 Tim 5:10, instead of 'if she has not refused to be a widow, having had children.' If she has welcomed strangers, making it evident that she is also called faithful even in marriage. If she has washed the feet of the saints, this he added to show that they must also be received with care. And it is evident that he says all these things as requiring them according to ability; for there is no one more perplexed than she who casts in the two obols.

Regarding 1 Tim 5:12, that having promised to remain to Christ, they later married. And regarding the first, he says 'faith' instead of 'first subjection,' and in ancient times 'first' meant the one being first and supreme and highest above all.
Regarding 1 Tim 5:17, teaching is the simple handing down through the words of the Scripture and the explanation of the meanings in the words.

title: The Manifestation of Sins and Good Works
english: And this is the word presenting the thoughts. Since he said above: do not quickly lay hands on anyone, nor share in the sins of others (1 Tim 5:24-25), now he tells the reason for which he said that. Not all sins are manifest; for many indeed sin while hiding it. He says therefore: test by time; for what is able to escape notice today is reproved tomorrow, and of the sins, some are manifest, leading to the judgment of men—for all will know that they sin and judge themselves unworthy—but after these things, some that are otherwise behaving seem unable to be hidden. Since therefore things are thus concerning men, do not quickly lay hands on anyone, lest you should ever be found sinning in what was hidden and be brought forward unworthily and share in that fall with him.

Likewise, good works are also manifest. Concerning good works he said this only, that they cannot be hidden—he did not say that they escape notice—but concerning evil works, some are manifest, and some escape notice. Why? Because no one quickly hides the good; for he who does the truth comes toward the light, but he who does evil hides, desiring to escape notice. The godly and faithful master has quickly stood to receive the benefits and goodwill of the slave, and being good, he becomes appreciative toward him. In order that those who receive the benefits do so, instead of those who are sensitive toward rewarding.

Just as fire is produced from the friction of stone and wood, so impiety is generated from the gathering of the wicked (1 Tim 6:5). It is not simply said of the one giving life, but so that he may remind us that the one giving life and giving revival to each, and who will give the reward to each worthily according to the time of the resurrection, since he was about to command the keeping according to the faith (1 Tim 6:13). And he did not simply set down the word; for if everything gives life, it is evident that he will make the godly men worthy also of the resurrection in the common giving of life, and of those denying bodies, giving the revival. Therefore, about to command that which is to keep the unspotted commandment, he reminds us of the one giving life, so that the hope of that life may urge toward godliness. And it is to be noted that he said 'the one giving life to all things,' not so that we should think him gives life even to the soulless. Such is also the case that all things came through him; for not all things in general, but the things about which the word is.

As the creatures remain in immortality and incorruption according to his grace and will, and desiring participation from him, even if they have a little nature of immortality like the angels, since this belongs principally to him alone (1 Tim 6:16), because he is self-life and the constitution and the supply of all good of the existing things.
